glossary.definition: A model exposing relevant operations and guarantees while hiding some implementation details. A queue abstraction defines FIFO behavior; a ring buffer is one possible representation of it. The abstraction should not promise guarantees the representation does not maintain.

A bound on the total cost of a sequence of operations expressed per operation. It is not a probability claim and does not mean each individual operation has the same latency. Geometric dynamic-array growth is the recurring example in this book.

A statement about growth as an input measure increases. It requires a chosen cost model and input-size definition. Big-O is an upper bound; it does not automatically specify a tight bound or a particular best, average, or worst case.

Access to an object owned elsewhere without taking ownership of its lifetime. References, pointers, iterators, and spans can act as borrows. The borrower must obey both lifetime and invalidation rules; non-nullness alone is not a lifetime proof.
Additional information allowing a claimed result to be checked. A route’s vertices can demonstrate feasibility and cost. A feasible route alone does not demonstrate that no cheaper route exists.

The transition at which a completed candidate replaces accepted state. Preparing a candidate first can preserve the old state on failure. The guarantee must name which state is protected; input consumption and external output are separate effects.

Two values are equivalent under an ordering when neither compares before the other. This can differ from operator==. Ordered containers and sorting stability must be understood in terms of the comparator actually supplied.
An exploration that accounts for every solution allowed by its model, either directly or through justified reductions. A heuristic that finds a useful result quickly is not automatically complete.
Comparing multiple implementations or models on the same inputs. Independence matters: two implementations sharing an incorrect recurrence may agree while both solve the wrong problem.

A property maintained at a designated boundary, such as before every loop iteration or after every public mutation. An invariant is useful when it explains what the representation means and supports the next operation, not merely when it restates that the program should work.

The loss of a borrow’s permitted relationship to a container after an operation. Reallocation can invalidate vector iterators even if a high-level operation later reports failure elsewhere. Logical value preservation and borrow preservation are distinct guarantees.
A property allowing an optimal solution to be assembled from appropriate optimal subproblem solutions. The chosen state must contain every constraint affecting future decisions.
A position dividing a sequence according to a predicate. Lower-bound search returns such a boundary; it does not by itself prove that a matching element exists at that position.
Omitting a search branch because a justified condition proves that it cannot contribute a required solution. Changing candidate order is a heuristic ordering decision, not necessarily pruning.

Preservation of relative order among records equivalent under the sorting comparator. It must be observed with identities or additional fields; sorting equal integers cannot expose an exchange of their indistinguishable positions.

The property that equal state descriptions imply equal future subproblems under the fixed context. A memoization key that omits remaining inventory can violate this property even when its numeric amount matches.

Replacing a candidate only when its objective value is better, not merely equal. In HarborRoutes this rule supports a simple deterministic predecessor policy and avoids rewriting equal-distance ancestry casually.
A deleted-slot marker that preserves an open-addressing probe path. It is available for future insertion but does not mean that lookup can stop as it would at a never-used slot.
